utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is case number IT-96-21-A, the Prosecutor versus Delalic and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We're up to group 5 and, Mr. Kuzmanovic, you're first off the rank here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This section of the argument deals with the principle of double jeopardy, and it was filed in a supplementary brief that Mr. Moran and I did about two or three months ago, and it came about as a result of the Kupreskic trial judgement. This issue revolves around convictions that Mr. Mucic and Mr. Delic had, and sentences for grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions and for violations of the laws and customs of war based upon the same acts. It is our position that the Kupreskic trial judgement, in section 5(D) paragraphs 637 to 748 is applicable, and we believe that the Appeals Chamber should adopt that section and vacate the -- one of the two convictions, either for grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions and for -- or for violations of the laws or customs of war when the elements of each offence are the same. The Kupreskic Trial Chamber adopted the double jeopardy test announced by the United States Supreme Court in Blockburger versus United States. I have supplied, through Mr. Hocking, copies of the Blockburger case for you, Your Honours, as well as a more recent pronouncement in which this principle has been upheld, and the same circumstance even if sentences are concurrent, which is what we have in this case, and that Supreme Court is Ball versus United States, which is a case decided in 1995. Incidentally, these cases are available for free on the Internet at a site called caselaw.com. The reason behind -- by the way, the Prosecution has also received copies of the two cases as well. The reasoning behind the United States Supreme Court's decision in Ball, which followed the court's holding in Blockburger, was that the appropriate inquiry is whether each provision requires proof of a fact which the other does not. And the only remedy the United States enumerated was that court within which sentencing responsibility resides must exercise its discretion and vacate one of the underlying convictions. One of the convictions as well as its concurrent sentence was considered by the Ball Court to be unauthorised punishment for a separate offence. And significantly, the United States Supreme Court reasoned that a second conviction, whose concomitant sentence is served concurrently, doesn't evaporate because of the concurrence of the sentence. Page 865 of Ball -- a little factual background on Ball. In the Ball case, the person was arrested. The police found him in possession of another person's firearm that was reported missing. This person threatened a neighbour with the firearm and he tried unsuccessfully to sell it. The person was then indicted on charges of receiving a firearm and possessing a firearm in violation of two federal statutes. He was convicted at the Trial-Court level on both counts and he was sentenced to consecutive terms of imprisonment on each count. The Court of Appeals then remanded the case to the district court saying it was violative of Blockburger and instructed the Trial Court to modify the sentences not to have them consecutive but to have them concurrent. And the United States Supreme Court held that that violated the principle of double jeopardy, despite the fact that these sentences were concurrent, because the elements of each act were essentially one in the same. In our argument in this case, for purposes of the double jeopardy principle here and how it applies is based upon the Kupreskic trial judgement and its adoption of the Blockburger test. Mucic, and for that matter any accused, in our opinion, cannot be convicted of both a grave breach and a violation based upon the same acts. For example, in the indictment, Mr. Mucic, under Article 7(3), was held to be responsible under Count 13, for example, with wilful killing, which is a grave breach under Article 2(A) of the Statute. Under Count 14, he was held to be responsible of a violation of the laws or customs of war, punishable under Article 3 of the Statute. Both of the violations were for acts and omissions as a superior. Because wilful killing and murder, in our opinion, and I believe in the opinion of the -- even the trial judgement in Celebici, are essentially one in the same, we believe the Appeals Chamber should vacate one of the convictions in each instance where he or Mr. Delic were convicted of both a grave breach and violations of the laws or customs of war based upon the same conduct. In fact, the Celebici Trial Chamber itself, in paragraph 433, stated, and I quote: "The ordinary meaning of the English term 'murder' is also understood as something more than manslaughter and thus, as stated above, no difference of consequence flows from the use of wilful killing in place of murder." That same trial judgement also stated in paragraph 439 that the mens rea required to establish crimes of wilful killing and murder is present where there is demonstrated an intention on the part of the accused to kill, inflict serious injury, in reckless regard of human life. For all intents and purposes, we submit, the Celebici Trial Chamber's definition of "wilful killing" and "murder" is one and the same. The Trial Chamber's judgement also defines two categories of "wilfully causing great suffering," et cetera, and "cruel treatment" almost identically in the judgement in paragraphs 511 and 552. Mr. Mucic was found guilty of a grave breach, wilfully causing great suffering or serious injury to body or health, and a violation of the laws or customs of war in respect to Slavko Susic, for example. Because the definitions of those two crimes under Article 2 and Article 3, at least in the Trial Chamber's judgement, are one and the same, we believe that that is violative of the principle of double jeopardy, and one of the two, either the grave breach or the violation of the laws or customs of war, should be vacated, again based upon the Trial Court's, in Kupreskic's, adoption of the Blockburger test. Other counts with respect to Mr. Mucic are 33 and 34. Thirty-three and thirty-four are both findings of guilt as a superior on a grave breach for torture and a violation of the laws or customs of war for torture. One of the two, we believe, should be vacated pursuant to the Blockburger test. It also applies in counts 38 and 39, counts 44 and 45, and 46 and 47 of the indictment. All of these categories are defined essentially the same way by the Trial Chamber in its judgement. "Wilfully causing," that phrase, and "cruel treatment," at paragraphs 511 and 552 of the Trial Chamber's judgement, and "inhuman treatment," at paragraph 543 of the Trial Court Chamber's judgement, are essentially defined in the same way. For those reasons, Your Honours, we believe this Appeal Chamber should accept the Kupreskic adoption of the Blockburger test with respect to double jeopardy and vacate one of each of the double convictions for Mr. Mucic and Mr. Delic based upon the same acts. We also believe that the Appeals Chamber should adopt paragraphs 742 to 748 of the Kupreskic judgement, which demonstrates the methodology to deal with this issue at the Trial Chamber level. It is essentially a pleadings and practice section of the Kupreskic judgement which discusses cumulative charging: when it is appropriate for a prosecutor to add a charge with the leave of court, without leave of court, and what some of the results of those decisions could be. And with that, Your Honours, I will, unless there are any questions, I will pass to my colleague on the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Before you sit down, you would agree, I suppose, that it's a very separate issue in relation to separate charging. Even if all of your arguments are correct about separate convicting, separate charging seems to throw out completely different issues. It's certainly not something we have to determine here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, Your Honour. I believe the Kupreskic decision does talk about separate charging, the Trial Chamber's decision, and I think that the approach elucidated in the Kupreskic judgement in those paragraphs which I cited is appropriate. The Court does or does not have to adopt that, as an Appeals Chamber, as a practice for the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: My point was: We don't have to decide it in this appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The second question which I would like to ask you: Has any other country adopted the United States' view that double jeopardy can arise within the one case rather than successive cases?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you off the top of my head, Your Honour, but I know that at least in England the double jeopardy principle does apply with respect to what happens shortly after sentence. And Mr. Morrison can address that issue specifically if you'd like, but the Trial Chamber's judgement in the Kupreskic case does go over several --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We've read the Kupreskic judgement. But I was asking whether any other country -- and I don't think the United Kingdom has -- adopted the United States' view that double jeopardy can arise in the same case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know of any country, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And the third question: What do you suggest is the approach that the Court should take in determining which conviction to keep? Is it the most serious offence, and if so, how do you work that out? Is it the one which is the most specific? Is it the one which in relation to which there is the most evidence or the most offences that have been committed, which are all within the one charge?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I would think, Your Honour, it would be the one where there is the most evidence. And the reason I say that is the way the Chamber defined "murder" and "wilful killing," if you read them side by side or look at them side by side, they're essentially the same, so my estimation would be it would be the evidence and the amount of evidence that's there that would be dispositive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Would you agree that it would be the offence which leads to the most appropriate sentence, in other words, which encompasses the greatest amount of conduct on the part of the particular accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. Mr. Morrison would like to add just a comment in answer to one of your questions, if you'd like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's simply to assist on the question you posed to Mr. Kuzmanovic as to whether any other country had adopted the question of double jeopardy in a single case. All I can speak of is as to the practice in the United Kingdom, where you have, for instance, a Prosecution, and I prosecute more than I defend, for, say, conspiracy, where within the facts of the case there are also substantive offences which are identifiable. And if an indictment is placed before the Court which contains counts of conspiracy and also counts of substantive offences, the practice has grown up now and is followed rigorously that counsel for the Crown are obliged to indicate before trial whether they wish to proceed on the conspiracy or the substantive counts, and they are only in rare occasions allowed to proceed upon both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. That's certainly the practice in other countries as well, but that isn't really double jeopardy. It relies on a completely different issue, at least as explained by other superior courts of appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: It is, but there is an analogy. As far as the defendant is concerned, from the defendant's point of view, he would see it as a double jeopardy point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may shock the Court, but I don't have anything to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Staker?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: May it please the Chamber. The brief filed by Mr. Mucic and Mr. Delic on this ground of appeal on the 14th of February this year contained only three pages of submissions in relation to this ground of appeal, and those three pages contained essentially only one single argument, which was that cumulative convictions under Article 2 and Article 3 were inconsistent with the Kupreskic judgement. We concede that the Appeals Chamber has a power of de novo review on issues of law, but nevertheless, where an error of law is alleged, it remains the case that the Trial Chamber's judgement will stand unless the error is established, so the appellant still has a burden of persuasion. The invocation of the Kupreskic judgement by the appellants is capable of a very short answer. The Kupreskic judgement is a decision of the Trial Chamber. It's not binding even on other Trial Chambers, and it's certainly not binding on the Appeals Chamber. That judgement establishes a legal test for cumulative convictions, which has not been applied in any other decision of any Chamber of this Tribunal or the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, and in certain respects it's directly contradicted by the practice of other Trial Chambers, and even of the Appeals Chamber itself in the Tadic appeal judgement. The Kupreskic judgement itself doesn't even address the possibility of cumulative convictions under Article 2 and Article 3, and there was no express finding in relation to that issue in the Kupreskic judgement. I'd refer to paragraph 4.80 of the Prosecution brief in relation to the cumulative conviction issue that sets out further difficulties with the Kupreskic judgement. And the Prosecution submits that for that reason alone, the brief filed by the appellants doesn't discharge the burden of persuasion in establishing an error by the Trial Chamber in this case. But despite the availability of such a short answer, the Prosecution brief that was filed on this issue contains some 50 pages of submissions on this issue. The reason for such detail was that the issue of cumulative convictions is one of general importance in the practice of this Tribunal. It's arisen on numerous occasions in both tribunals and it's never been the subject of a definitive pronouncement by the Appeals Chamber. Therefore, in an effort to assist the Appeals Chamber, we've sought to address the issue in a more comprehensive way. I should point out materially similar submissions are also before the Appeals Chamber in the Prosecution appeal brief in the Kayishema and Ruzindena case and similar submissions may be put by the Prosecution in other appeals. The brief, I submit, speaks for itself. I needn't go through a 50-page brief in any detail, but I would mention a few points. My first point is one of terminology. For the purposes of these proceedings, the issue has been given the label "cumulative convictions," but that's not really a term of art in any legal system that I'm --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Staker please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: In civil-law systems, on the other hand, there is an established terminology. In French, this is an issue which would be referred to as "concours d'infractions," which might be more accurately translated into English as "concurrence of offences" or "concurrence of crimes." Similar terminology is used in other civil-law systems. Civil-law systems generally also distinguish between what is called "real concurrence" and what is called "ideal concurrence", ideal concurrence being the situation where a single act of an accused violates more than one provision of the criminal law, which is the situation before us now. In our brief, we have, to a degree, adopted the civil-law terminology. One reason is convenience. The expression "ideal concurrence" is much shorter and simpler than the expression "situations in which a single act of the accused violates more than one provision of the criminal law." Another reason is that this civil-law terminology is found in some of the decisions of this Tribunal and the Rwanda Tribunal which deal with the issue. The convenience might also be highlighted by Mr. Kuzmanovic's reference to the issue of double jeopardy. I would submit that the issue of double jeopardy is one which is well established in civil-law systems also, but there is as well a concept of ideal concurrence. So the use of this expression distinguishes between the two. At the same time, we're conscious that the use of this sort of terminology may cause confusion in the extent -- to the extent that it may suggest that the rules applicable in this Tribunal are the same as the rules that apply in any particular national system. In fact, our submission is that the rules governing ideal concurrence differ significantly, even within civil-law systems. For instance, my understanding is that in France, the general rule of ideal concurrence, and I understand this is also subject to exceptions, but the general rule is that an accused cannot be convicted of more than one crime for a single act. In Germany, on the other hand, the general rule of ideal concurrence, which is set out in paragraph 4.92 of our brief, is that the Court will make findings in respect of every crime that has been committed by the one act. However, in Germany, under paragraph 52 subparagraph (2) of the Criminal Code, only a single sentence is imposed, which is determined by reference to the sentence prescribed for the most serious of the offences. In other civil-law systems, the position is different again. In paragraph 4.93 of our brief, we give examples of countries where, in case of ideal concurrence, the maximum sentence fixed for the most serious crime can be increased to take account of the fact that the act constituted more than one crime. And it may not be without significance that the systems adopting this approach include, in addition to Bulgaria, Denmark, Italy, Portugal, and Switzerland, the former Yugoslavia itself. Thus while the expression "ideal concurrence" is used in all these legal systems to describe the issue, the solution adopted to the issue varies from country to country. Mr. Kuzmanovic has referred us to the practice in the United States, where the Blockburger test is applied. That's yet another approach again. The Blockburger test prevents cumulative convictions for the same conduct but only in certain particular circumstances, which is where this test of reciprocal speciality is not satisfied. The Prosecution submits that one of the fundamental errors in the reasoning of the Kupreskic judgement is that it tries to find a solution to the issue of ideal concurrence by identifying general principles of law common to national legal systems. This approach was indicated in paragraph 668 [sic]of the Kupreskic judgement. The Trial Chamber indicated its intention to rely on the principles common to the various legal systems of the world, in particular those shared by most civil-law and common-law criminal systems. Then in paragraph 677, there's a similar reference to general principles of criminal law as they derive from the convergence of the principal penal system of the world. For the reasons given, it is submitted that that approach is somewhat artificial because the similarity between the systems is not as great as the Kupreskic judgement would suggest. The Prosecution submits that the approach taken by the Kupreskic judgement can be contrasted with that taken by the Appeals Chamber in its judgement of 15 July 1999 in the Tadic appeal dealing with the common purpose doctrine. In paragraphs 185 to 283 [sic] of that judgement, which cover some 20 pages, the Appeals Chamber considers the International Humanitarian Law authorities in relation to the issue, decisions of national and international courts dealing with war crimes cases, international treaties, and a decision of this Tribunal, and it was only after dealing with all those international authorities, it then, in paragraph 224, made reference to certain national law authorities, but it added in the following paragraph, and I quote: "It should be emphasised that reference to national legislation and case law only serves to show that the notion of common purpose upheld in international criminal law has an underpinning in many national systems. By contrast, in the area under discussion, national legislation and case law cannot be relied upon as a source of international principles of rules, under the doctrine of the general principles of law recognised by the nations of the world: for this reliance to be permissible, it would be necessary to show that most, if not all, countries adopt the same notion of common purpose. More specifically, it would be necessary to show that, in any case, the major legal systems of the world take the same approach to this notion. The above brief survey shows that this is not the case." The Prosecution, therefore, submits that the answer to the issue of ideal concurrence should be sought not by reference to national legal systems. There is now an extensive body of case law of both international Tribunals in relation to cases of ideal concurrence, and the Prosecution submits that the questions to be asked are, first, whether any consistent principles can be derived from the existing jurisprudence of the Tribunals, and if so, why there is any reason the Appeals Chamber should exist [sic] from the existing practice and principles. As to the first question, the practice of the two international Tribunals, in relation to ideal concurrence, is quite extensive. It's set out in detail at paragraphs 4.9 to 4.72 in our brief. It's conceded that much of this jurisprudence consists of decisions of Trial Chambers which are not binding upon the Appeals Chamber and some of which are the subject of pending appeals. Nevertheless, where extensive practice already exists at the Trial Chamber level, when a matter is first considered by the Appeals Chamber, the Appeals Chamber should not, it is submitted, ignore that practice when deciding the matter. Although not bound by Trial Chamber decisions, such decisions can be persuasive, especially if a body of jurisprudence constante has already begun to become established. The practice of entering cumulative convictions under Articles 2 and 3 in respect of the same conduct also finds support in the decision of the Appeals Chamber in the Tadic appeal judgement. Details are given in paragraphs 4.11 and 4.12 of our brief. The particular issue of cumulative convictions under Article 2 and Article 3, the possibility of such cumulative convictions also finds support in decisions of this Tribunal at the Trial Chamber level. I refer to paragraph 4.80, subparagraph (6) of the Prosecution brief, on page 48. The Kupreskic judgement itself concerned cumulative convictions under Article 3 and Article 5 of the Statute. Its specific findings in that respect are inconsistent with the practice of the Appeals Chamber in the Tadic appeal judgement and the Jelisic and the Blaskic judgements. I refer again to paragraph 4.80 of our brief. We, therefore, submit that the Kupreskic judgement cannot be considered an authoritative statement on principles of cumulative convictions in the legal system of this Tribunal. As our brief acknowledges, the Chambers of the two Tribunals have not been consistent in the way that they articulate the applicable principles in the legal system of this Tribunal. I refer to paragraph 4.78 of our brief, which identifies four and possibly five different tests that have been applied by different Chambers. But a test which the Prosecution submits is consistent with the weight of precedent in the Tribunal is effectively the Akayseu test, which on its face is somewhat narrower than what we call the Tadic test, although we submit that the Tadic test can be read in a way that it can be reconciled with the Akayseu test. On that I refer to paragraph 4.82 and 4.83 of our brief. Under this test, it is acceptable to convict the accused of two offences in relation to the same set of facts in the following circumstances: (1) where the offences have different elements; (2) where the provisions creating the offences protect different interests; or (3) where it's necessary to record a conviction for both offences in order to fully describe what the accused did. The Prosecution submits that under this test, an accused can always be charged with and convicted of more than one crime in respect of the same conduct if the different crimes fall under different Articles of the Statute. For the purposes of this case at least, this means that an accused can be convicted in respect of the same conduct of both the crime under Article 2 and under Article 3. There are three bases for the conclusion that cumulative convictions under Article 2 and Article 3 are consistent with the Akayesu test. First, there's the practice of the Tribunal itself. I've indicated that such cumulative convictions do find support in the existing practice, and the test should be interpreted and applied in a way that is consistent with the existing practice. Secondly, for the reasons set out in our brief, we submit that each of the Articles of the Tribunal's Statute protects different interests for the purposes of this test. I refer to paragraph 4.85 of our brief. And we would submit that in any event, where an act constitutes a crime under both Article 2 and Article 3 of the Statute, it can be said that it's necessary to record a conviction for both offences in order fully to describe what the accused did for the purposes of this test. The second question, which I indicated earlier, is whether there is any reason why this existing practice should not continue to be followed. Is the practice inconsistent with the rights of the accused? The Prosecution submits the answer's no, for the reasons given in paragraph 4.89 of our brief. We submit that it does not violate the principle of non bis in idem or double jeopardy for an accused to be convicted of more than one crime in respect of the same conduct at the same trial as opposed to successive trials for the same conduct. The legal systems that I have referred to earlier and the authorities set out in our brief indicate that that conclusion is supported by practice in various jurisdictions. It may be that some jurisdictions take a different view. Mr. Kuzmanovic referred to the United States practice, which indicates that this would be regarded as inconsistent with double jeopardy in the United States, at least in the limited circumstances where the Blockburger test applies. And the question was asked whether there was any country that takes the same approach. I could perhaps assist the Chamber by pointing out that to the best my knowledge, and I can't say this with certainty, I mentioned earlier that in France, cumulative convictions for the same or more than one conviction for the same act, as a general rule, is not permitted, and I understand that the rationale given for that in France is a double jeopardy or non bis in idem rationale. But the other examples we give from civil law systems, such as Germany and the former Yugoslavia itself, we submit indicates that a contrary approach is not inconsistent with international standards. We further submit that the practice is not inconsistent with judicial efficiency, for the reasons given in paragraph 4.90 of our brief. Whether the multiple crimes are charged cumulatively or in the alternative, it's still necessary for the Prosecution to bring evidence of all of the elements of the crimes charged. The Prosecution concedes that there are some limitations on the possibility of cumulative convictions. Again we refer to paragraph 4.8, subparagraph 3, paragraph 4.76, and paragraph 4.88 of our brief, which deals with the concept of apparent concurrence, as it's referred to in civil law systems. We give the example of an accused who is charged with stabbing a victim to death. We concede that in respect of that one act, the accused couldn't be convicted of both murder and wilfully causing great suffering or serious injury to the victim. Once the serious injury leads to the death of the victim, the murder would absorb the crime of serious injury. And this kind of limitation is expressly acknowledged in the Akayesu judgement at paragraph 468. But the Prosecution submits that this type of limitation only applies to crimes within the same article of the Tribunal Statute. Each article of the Statute is not a lesser included offence of another, or a different form of participation of another, and for the reasons given, it's submitted that convictions under two different articles for the same conduct is permissible in this Tribunal's legal system, and accordingly we submit that this ground of appeal should be rejected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: From a practical point of view, could you explain what is the difference between the second and the third indicia in -- I think it's pronounced the Akayesu judgement. What is the difference between them, that is, the different interests affected in order to describe more fully what the accused did?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: That may be a difficult question to answer in the abstract, Your Honour, and it may be that it's the sort of thing that would be developed through further jurisprudence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You don't think that one includes the other and that you're accumulating the two where one would do?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: It may depend on how you defined "different social interests," Your Honour. It may be that if one took a slightly narrower view of different social interests, that the third limb would then provide a practical solution where it's clear that a single conviction would simply not reflect the nature of what occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It's our submission that concurrence may be ideal for the Prosecution, but we are talking about punishment twice, for two charges which are essentially defined identically, and that, I believe, is fundamentally unfair. I will submit that the issue of the Akayesu test is relevant here, and let's apply it to this case. My colleague said that the offence must have different elements, and I submit to you that murder, under Article 2 -- or wilful killing and murder, under Articles 2 and 3, are essentially one and the same. The Trial Chamber in our case decided them or defined them the same. Number 2, provisions creating offences predict different interests. I think that's important here. Yesterday we've heard from the -- with regard to Common Article 3 that the Prosecution said Common Article 3 was there to provide protection in internal conflicts where grave breaches are not available. So then the issue becomes, where the conflict is international, can you convict them of both? And I think number 2 fails when we look at it in our case. And obviously number 3, record conditions to fully describe what the accused did, that is an element of that Akayesu test which I think can be fulfilled by the Trial Chamber, and probably was in this case, given the lengthy discussion about the conditions to fully describe what each accused did. But I think the second element of the Akayesu test, provisions creating offences to protect different interests, fails, and I think therefore the charges are cumulative simply because of the position taken on Common Article 3, internal versus international: Where the conflict is international, can you then be convicted of both? Is that cumulative? And I believe that it is. And that's all I have in reply, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We move into group 6. Mr. Morrison, we have been informed informally that the omission of what was originally ground 12 was accidental and that ground 12 is still relied upon. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. It was an accidental omission from the final issues that were, I think, sent by my learned friend into the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Providentially it can retain the same number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Essentially, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The other matter I thought I should raise with you before you commence: You have referred to various sections of the PACE legislation, and the Prosecution seems to be very sensitive to these matters. Is there any objection to us saying what is obviously a clearly up-to-date version of the PACE legislation which has been set out in the submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think our position on that was set out in our response brief, and we say that if national legislation or case law is relied upon as persuasive authority in support of a legal argument, there's no objection to it simply being referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: This is your distinction you draw between that and the constitution of Costa Rica?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If you're actually seeking some relief based on the fact of national law, it must be proved --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So there's no need to prove the PACE legislation here?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I've been referring to national jurisprudence and practice myself in my submissions just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm much obliged for the fact that I don't have to prove the PACE legislation. I notice the time given for this section by Mr. Hocking was very generously extended to one hour. I can, I hope to everybody's relief, say that it's going to be a very great deal less than that. But there's one point, if I be forgiven for one moment trespassing back in time, because sometimes when one hears things said at the time, they make a lot of sense and you're not in agreement with them; then you think about them a bit more and a word takes on or a phrase takes on a different meaning. I got an e-mail the other day setting out some responses by children to a religious education examination, and one child wrote this: "Christians can only have one wife. This is known as monotony." The illustration by the Prosecution of the effective indemnity for a constitutionally superior commander in the body of Her Majesty, Queen Elizabeth the Second, is flawed by their own position that a person of influence may be liable under Article 7(3), because whatever the constitutional limitations upon Her Majesty acting outside the authority of being the Queen in parliament, which is how she does, in fact, derive her authority, the monarch would no doubt be a person not only of influence, but of considerable influence, having, as the monarch does, the extra-parliamentary power to confer commissions of officers of her armed forces and to award honours for civil and military services to the Crown. So one could envisage a situation where a military commander did a certain act which was going to be alleged to be a crime but had been awarded by Her Majesty, out of her own writ, of one of her personal Honours, for instance, the order of the Royal Victorian Order, and she may then be seen as a person of influence for others who would go on to commit similar offences, if offence it was. And that, in my submission, illustrates the serious flaw in the pursuit of the person-of-influence approach. I move on. The admissibility of the OTP interviews. This in many ways may be otiose as far as both the Defence and the crown are concerned, to this extent: that we are still unsure as to what the effect is going to be of the additional information which may or may not yet be put before this Honourable Tribunal. And I accept that it may be that the thrust of the argument here as to the admission of the second of the two interviews we're dealing with may or may not be of moment. But there is a general issue which the Defence raise on behalf of Mr. Mucic which we say is of general and future application. The objective, we submit, is to be fair, whatever the consequences, when one is considering what somebody says in an interview, which is of course pre-trial, and usually, in most jurisdictions, pre-indictment, but not necessarily as far as this Tribunal is concerned. And if the objective is to be fairness, that fairness cannot be subjugated to any intellectually superior or acceptable argument or to partisan compromise. The jurisprudence in respect of the admissibility of the interviews or, for instance, the identification of suspects, or for searches, is in constant evolvement, and one doesn't have to look very far back in time in my own jurisdiction to see that. Prior to PACE it was an accepted procedure that a defendant would be interviewed by the police, usually by two police officers. There would be no tape recording of the interview. The officers would simply sit and ask questions. At the conclusion of the interview, which may have been hours in length, those two officers would go away, and in the words hallowed in many cases, make up their notes, together. This was not only a course to which no objection was taken; it was a course which was followed case in and case out. And we used to have trials where Judges would solemnly address jurors that police officers had trained minds and could do this. Well, in some of the cases that one appeared in, and some of the officers that appeared in front of you, one would legitimately wonder where their minds had been trained, because you would have somebody saying, for instance, after a two-hour interview, that he could remember verbatim what the defendant said and what the questions were. This was patent nonsense, but it was adopted in case after case. And I recall that when PACE was first mooted and the suggestion was that each interview was going to be tape recorded, there was outrage in some police quarters, and I recall an article in the police review at about that time stating solemnly that there would never be another conviction in the Crown court if this were to happen. Well, as it happens, the statistics show us that since PACE, actually the conviction rate has crept up, not gone down. The Miranda provisions in the United States and the litigation which was flowed therefrom is another example of how this is an evolving part of jurisprudence. The fundamental problem that's been adopted, in my respectful submission, in cases hitherto is the adoption of an objective approach to the admission of interviews and to the reliability of what a person has said in those interviews, particularly in the case, as in Mr. Mucic's case, where he was not, in fact, legally represented in the interviews. And the reason it may be a particular problem in cases before this Tribunal, at trial, certainly, is that in the majority of cases in any national jurisdiction, a defendant is likely to be linguistically and culturally at ease, and an objective case may well be fair. That is unlikely to be the case where people from the former Yugoslavia are being interviewed. It is correspondingly very unlikely that the social turmoil that underscored the events that have given rise to the formation of this Tribunal would be apparent in a national context. So although I accept and I have set out in the brief that in many cases, and in particular that of the United Kingdom, the test is essentially an objective test. It is essentially, in my submission, the issue having been raised before this Appellate Tribunal, is to see whether or not that is a test which should stand or whether or not it should be -- there should be a move towards a more subjective test of such interviews. To be fair, which must include a determination of the qualitative aspect of fairness, i.e., the foundation that the Prosecution bear the burden of proof to the standard of beyond a reasonable doubt, means that you have, in my submission, to look at matters subjectively. The fact that somebody is being interviewed in a language other than his, probably in a jurisdiction or a place which he has no cultural or personal knowledge, and the fact that he is being interviewed about matters which have arisen from an extraordinary and extra-national set of circumstances, in our submission, is very germane. I don't seek to say anything else about the admissibility of the interviews now, because it's set out in the briefs, but it seems to us, on behalf of Mr. Mucic, that when you have a man who is being interviewed in a language, in a jurisdiction far removed from a jurisdiction which he understood, to wit, Austria, he was initially being interviewed in a language which he did not understand, although of course it was in translation for him, and he was being interviewed without a lawyer present, and there is a debate in the papers which can be resolved upon the papers as to whether he should or should not have been represented and whether that was a wilful error on his part or a deliberate decision on his part not to be represented. That's another matter. But if one is going to take as the base point complete fairness, it is our submission that the time has come to move towards a subjective approach to interviews and away from a national approach to interviews, where the legislation and where the procedures have been adopted and adapted over many, many years, and where, as I say, the conditions and the cultural influences upon a suspect are likely to be very, very different than they are upon Mr. Mucic in particular, but defendants before these tribunals in particular. I go on to the second ground, which is the conduct of defence errors by counsel at trial. Now, I've spoken to my learned friend Mr. Staker about this, because he was concerned, as indeed I was concerned. It doesn't, in fact, amount to a ground of appeal by Mr. Mucic of ineffective representation by counsel. That was something that was considered, but it is apparent that that is not being now raised. The reason it's being raised at all is this: That the Trial Chamber, in their judgement, chose to mention the conduct of the Defence. The judgement is not simply a historical narrative of the trial, it is a judgement. It is not a judgement of counsel, it's a judgement of the defendant. Therefore, it can only be assumed, on behalf of Mr. Mucic, that there was a reason for raising the matters which the Trial Chamber did raise in paragraph 75 of the judgement. On any analysis, it amounts to an effective publication of criticism of his then lead counsel. All I seek to say, on behalf of Mr. Mucic, is this: If there is any good reason or any merit in the Trial Chamber having so set out those criticisms, they are criticisms of his counsel, they are not criticisms of the appellant, and we would simply ask that when this judgement is read or reread, that this learned Appellate Tribunal ignores them completely. There cannot be any proper basis for having included those, in our submission, in the judgement. There is certainly no proper basis for criticism of Mr. Mucic by virtue of them. That leads on to the third ground of unlawful confinement. I don't propose a rerun of any question of protected persons upon this, but there is one point which arises. It's been argued in the brief and responded to by the Prosecution, and I don't want to take those matters any further. I do have -- I want to refer to the particular paragraph in the judgement that sets out the reasoning. It's paragraph 1145. It's short and I read it: "The Trial Chamber has established that Zdravko Mucic was in a position of de facto position of superior authority over the Celebici prison camp. The Trial Chamber finds that Zdravko Mucic, by virtue of this position, was the individual with primary responsibility for and had the ability to effect the continued detention of civilians in the prison camp. Specifically, Zdravko Mucic, in this position, had the authority to release detainees. By omitting to ensure that a proper inquiry was undertaken into the status of the detainees and that those civilians who could not lawfully be detained were immediately released, Zdravko Mucic participated in the unlawful confinement of civilians in the Celebici prison camp. "Accordingly, the Trial Chamber finds Zdravko Mucic guilty pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute of the unlawful confinement of civilians as charged under Count 48 of the indictment." We reach this position: That he has been found guilty on command responsibility, superior responsibility under Article 7(3). The, of course, specific difference between Article 7(1) and 7(3) in this context is "know or had reason to know." The omission contained within 7(3), "had reason to know," has been used as a basis for the positive finding of mens rea under Article 7(1). It must be, if one reads and gives natural meaning to the words in paragraph 1145, that what the Trial Chamber is saying is that the defendant Mucic had the active mens rea; he knew or -- not must have known but knew that there were detainees in the camp who were not lawfully detained. Now, there is all the difference in the world between unlawful detention and unlawful treatment. One cannot make the jump from saying that there were people in the camp who are unlawfully treated or may have been unlawfully treated that they were, therefore, unlawfully initially detain. And it is a counsel of perfection, in our submission, to say that Zdravko Mucic, that while he may be convicted under section 73 of "ought to have known," that can be translated into a positive mens rea under 7(1) that he did know, and the adoption and assumption is made that he had the power to know. It's been stated in the brief, and I restate it, simply this: That the fact that somebody is a guard, even a superior amongst guards in a prison camp is not the same thing as a person who has the authority or the knowledge or the status to take somebody into custody ab initio. A person who arrives at a prison, particularly in a time of social turmoil and hostilities, can be, in my submission, taken to be a person who has been lawfully detained as far as the guards of that camp are concerned, and it is a counsel of impossible perfection that in those circumstances somebody could be expected to conduct an individual inquiry as to the lawfulness of each person's arrest and to determine, on each case, that that person should be released against the effective authority of the person who has already authorised their detention. There is no evidence in this case that Zdravko Mucic, whatever his authority, had greater authority than the person or persons who authorised the detention of the inmates at Celebici camp. To make the assumption that he did is both wrong and, in our submission, unfair, and that is what's happened in this case. Your Honour, those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Morrison, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I gather from what you said that if Mucic was not responsible for the unlawful confinement, not being the decision-maker, he could still be responsible for the unlawful treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: There is a plain distinction, in my submission, Your Honour, between the two. A person can be lawfully taken into confinement and then unlawfully treated when he's in confinement. The unlawful treatment does not vitiate the lawfulness of the confinement in the first place. Otherwise, we would have a situation where if an individual prisoner was beaten up by a prison guard, he would be liable to be released from prison. That would be a logical non sequitur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So in that case, the case of unlawful treatment, he will not need even to discuss the issue of being in a commanding position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, first of all, in any individual's case you need to find out that the person was in a position of authority. So as far as each individual defendant is concerned, it would be necessary to be satisfied that the person was, in fact, in a position of authority. In this case, that's been found under Article 7(3), as far as Mr. Mucic is concerned. Only if the Appellate Chamber was satisfied that he was in such a position of authority would you then move on to say that being he's in a position of authority and had inter alia the power to release people did he then participate non-lawful confinement by not releasing or not putting into place a system by which people could be released. The one must -- as far as individual responsibility is concerned, individual culpability, the one must precede the other in his individual case. But, of course, I accept that a person can be lawfully detained and, thereafter, unlawfully treated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And, of course -- now we're speaking about unlawful treatment. This would perhaps be the bottom line, that even if he's not a commanding position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But if he was, if he had some authority, the fact that -- the idea is that confinement should be limited only to those who threaten the security of the state or of the whole country, not any civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: That goes back to the fundamental argument, if you're going to convict somebody under 7(1), that you find a positive mens rea in his case. In a situation of social turmoil and hostilities such as this was at this time, I repeat my submission that it is a counsel of impossible perfection to expect anybody to be able to conduct that sort of exercise in the heat of the moment or even given a few days. Where a number of people, a large number of people are confined, it would be necessary for an analysis of each person's status, of the background of each person to hear and determine perhaps evidence against that person, to hold some form of judicial inquiry. There can't be any sensible suggestion, in my submission, that that falls upon a person who is in the position of a guard or leader of guards of a camp. It may well fall upon a person who is an overall tactical commander or administrator in the area, and perhaps such an exercise should have been undertaken, but nobody suggested that this -- there's been assumption that this appellant has had that authority. There isn't a shred of evidence to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just for the sake of argument, in case the person has authority, and you are speaking about the heat of the moment, of course, in the heat of the moment you can't collect everybody even without having -- when there is a doubt, but then if there is some kind of length of time, there is enough opportunity to review and to -- and not to maintain the confinement of innocent people, of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: And we then find ourselves -- or certainly the Defence finds itself in the rather, at the moment, difficult position to determine, because at the moment, the length of time by which it would be proper to find, if it were proper to find at all that Mr. Mucic had responsibility for the camp, may well depend upon the documentation that has yet to be produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Morrison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Morrison. Mr. Staker again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: May it please the Chamber, in relation to this ground of appeal -- when I say "this ground of appeal," I mean the ground of the appeal relating to the admissibility of the interviews with the Office of the Prosecutor -- the starting point, as in the case of all grounds of appeal, must be what the standard of review is before this Appellate Chamber and in determining that, again the starting point is that there are a number of different kinds of decisions that may be made by a Trial Chamber when determining this kind of issue. One is the legal definition of the expression "voluntarily" in Rule 42(B). That, of course, is a question of law. A second matter is to determine what the actual events and circumstances of the case were. That's a question of fact. And the third matter that the Trial Chamber would have to consider is the application of the law to the facts and circumstances as established. We would submit that in making this -- a determination of this final matter, the Trial Chamber is required to weigh all the facts in evidence before it, and in some cases involving issues of this kind, it may be required to receive evidence and hear witnesses, and so in accordance with general principles, it would be necessary to afford a considerable margin of deference to the finding of the Trial Chamber, and it would only be where the decision of the Trial Chamber could be shown to be an abuse of discretion that there would be justification in the Appeals Chamber intervening on appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That, of course, puts back into your formula an issue of discretion as well. You hadn't asserted that earlier. You said there was, first of all, a question of law, then a question of fact as to voluntariness, then an application of the law to the facts. That's where the discretion would be exercised, do you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: It's discretionary in the sense that the application of the law to the facts isn't a mathematical process. It involves a degree of appreciation, and the appreciation is one for the Trial Chamber to make. It's the Chamber that has seen and heard the witnesses, and it's in the best position to determine the credibility and the best position to form a view of what the situation really was and what the position of the suspect would have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's an ordinary finding of fact in every case. Is there any overriding discretion such as is found in some legal systems that notwithstanding some error made by the Prosecution in some formula that it must follow, the Court, nevertheless, has a discretion to admit the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the answer to that would be found in the precise wording of the Rule of Procedure and Evidence that has been invoked in order to exclude the evidence of the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So that makes it a fourth issue, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. In relation to the question of the application of the law to the facts, whether the waiver of the right to counsel was voluntary, clearly the Chamber can't read an accused's mind and any evidence of a state of mind would have to be inferred from the objective circumstances as a whole. In this respect, we note that a test was, in fact, proposed in the appeal brief filed on behalf of Mr. Mucic in this case, a proposed test where the formulation was whether the conditions of the interrogation would be likely to lead a reasonable person to offer an involuntary confession or, for the purposes of this case, an involuntary waiver of counsel. The appeal brief states that this test is primarily an objective rather than a subjective test, although it's submitted that there must be an element of subjectivity in the case of a person who is under any form of disability or in a strange and unfamiliar situation, that is, in a foreign country or being questioned in a language that's not his own. The Prosecution doesn't concede that the mere fact a reasonable person is in a foreign country or is being interviewed in a language that is not his or her own, means that the conditions of detention would be likely to lead a reasonable person to waive their right to counsel involuntarily, but we understand this test to be saying that you look at what a reasonable person would be likely to have done in the particular circumstances, and that is essentially an objective test taking into account the relevant circumstances. In other words, it's a matter for the Trial Chamber to determine on the circumstances as a whole, and as I say, subject to review on the ground of unreasonableness. Now, the Prosecution submits that the decision of the Trial Chamber that excluded -- that refused to exclude the evidence of this interview with the Office of the Prosecutor isn't necessarily inconsistent with this test. The Defence argued before the Trial Chamber that Mr. Mucic, because of his cultural background, his lack of familiarity with Austrian culture and the procedures of the Tribunal, because of this he needed to have his rights explained to him in more detail. The Trial Chamber rejected this argument at paragraphs 58 to 60 of their decision, but it's submitted that at least on one reading of this decision it did this on the basis of the facts of the case rather than on the grounds of a particular legal test. It held that the rights of a suspect in the Tribunal's legal system are based on universal human rights, and that if these are explained to a suspect in a language that the suspect understands, they would be understood by the suspect even if they're different from the rights in any other particular legal system with which the suspect may be familiar. Therefore, there's no need to explain these rights to a suspect in a way that's more culturally specific to that suspect merely by virtue of that circumstance, and the Prosecution submits that this is a perfectly correct reasoning. Provided that the suspect's rights are explained in a language that the suspect understands, it shouldn't matter in what country the suspect is at the time, particularly in the case of an international tribunal which may interview suspects in many different countries and which has a legal system that's different to that in any particular national jurisdiction. If the rights in this Tribunal are based on universally recognised rights and they're explained through an interpreter in a language that the accused understands, unless there is some other circumstance that would indicate that a reasonable person, in all those circumstances, would be likely to involuntarily waive right to counsel, the inference must be that any waiver was voluntary. Now, the circumstances here were put before the Trial Chamber, and I take it that it's not contested by counsel for Mr. Mucic that when he was interviewed by the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor, he did have an interpreter at all times; that he was, before the interview began, informed of his rights under the Statute and Rules of the Tribunal, including his right to silence and his right to have a lawyer; and that he agreed to conduct an interview without the presence of an attorney; and that on several occasions during the course of that interview he was again informed of his rights under the Statute or the Rules, and he again agreed to proceed without an interpreter being present. The question then: Is there any circumstance -- sorry, I should add that -- the other facts that are mentioned in the Trial Chamber's judgement are, for instance, the fact that the accused had been living in Austria for several years at the time, and I don't think it would be in dispute, for instance, that he wasn't in a situation any more unusual than that of any other suspect being questioned by the police. He wasn't in the middle of a war zone. It wasn't a situation of civil disturbance. It was like any normal or regular situation where a person is arrested by the police pursuant to a regular warrant under Austrian law and questioned by the police. In circumstances such as that, we would submit it can't be unreasonable for a Trial Chamber, on the evidence, to reach the conclusion that the waiver of the right to have an attorney present was voluntary unless the accused brought evidence of some particular circumstance that might change the equation. And we submit that it's very significant that the accused in this case never brought any evidence as part of the application to exclude the evidence of the interview and, in particular, didn't even file an affidavit in support of the application despite, of course, being the person who had the primary knowledge of what the facts and circumstances were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Can you just help me there? Is there any procedure available for what some countries call a voir dire and others a somewhat more plebeian phrase, a trial within a trial, where the accused can give evidence in relation to the admissibility of material but cannot be cross-examined about the facts of the trial itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no such practice appears to have been established in this Tribunal to date, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There would be nothing to stop it though, would there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: There would be nothing to stop it. Where evidence is sought to be introduced, the Rules provide that the Chamber must determine its admissibility. At that stage, issues of admissibility could be taken up and the matter could be determined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, the very issue of whether or not something is voluntary is the prime example of where a voir dire is often taken, so that the complaint made that the interpreter was not allowed to be called, the basis of her being called being she was explain what was affecting his mind. That could have been answered by him quite clearly in a voir dire.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Yes. That is indeed our submission, Your Honour. We submit that the argument put on behalf of Mr. Mucic here is not based on any real evidence and the submissions are framed in terms of "likely" or "probably." There is simply no evidence that it was the case that there was any element present, in fact, that would have changed the balance of the equation which, as we say, as it was before the Trial Chamber, could reasonably lead to the conclusion - In fact, we would submit very reasonably lead to the conclusion - that the waiver of the right to counsel was voluntary. There is a suggestion that the second interview with the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor was somehow tainted by a prior interview with Austrian police officers. The interview with Austrian police officers was excluded on the ground that the accused did not have a lawyer present and under Austrian law and procedure was not entitled to have a lawyer present. That was held not to be consistent with the requirements of the procedures of this Tribunal. But in the appellant's brief at Registry page A738, paragraph (B), it's suggested that if an accused gives two interviews and his or her rights under Rule 42 are not respected at the first, then somehow, as a matter of logic, it affects the second interview, and we would submit there's nothing in logic that would inevitably lead to that conclusion. We would submit that even if one interview was not voluntary, as a matter of logic there is no reason why an accused or a suspect couldn't agree to give a second interview where the waiver of the right to counsel was voluntary. We, therefore, submit that it hasn't been demonstrated by the appellant that there was any error in the Trial Chamber's judgement in this respect. I would also, just in conclusion, note that the appeal brief here places very considerable reliance on the law of England and Wales which it sets out at length. This is the only national jurisdiction that it relies upon. With the greatest of respect to that jurisdiction, it is submitted that a decision of this Tribunal can't be erroneous merely because it's inconsistent with the law of one national jurisdiction. Reference to national jurisdictions may be useful for some purposes, but simply to point to the provisions of one is not sufficient. The appellant's appeal brief submits that the legal system of England and Wales is the system having the jurisprudence in relation to this ground of appeal following most closely upon the substance and spirit of the approach laid down in the relevant provision of the Statute and the Rules, but this is merely a bald submission that's not supported by any reasoning. And, in fact, the appellant's appeal brief goes on to freely admit that in England, Judges are pragmatic and, therefore, reluctant to articulate the principles lying behind the various rules behind the discretionary powers. And if the judges are reluctant to articulate the principles, it's submitted that it makes the value of such authorities all the more questionable before this Tribunal where analogies with national jurisdictions, of course, would be based on general principles. The reluctance to articulate general principles, I understand, is a comment frequently made about common-law systems by people from the civil-law tradition. I don't mean to suggest by that that authorities from common-law systems aren't of value before this Tribunal. They certainly are frequently referred to. But it is the general principles that need to be identified and articulated. Apart from those submissions, Your Honour, we would rely on our brief in relation to that ground of appeal. Unless there are questions, I'd propose to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: The next ground of appeal is the conduct of Defence counsel. It's our understanding this isn't a ground of appeal at all. Our submission is that the inference can't be drawn that the Trial Chamber was necessarily trying to criticise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think, as Mr. Morrison very frankly said, the only point of raising it is to make sure we take no notice [Realtime transcript read in error "take notice"] of what was said in the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Our response to that would be we don't think there's any suggestion that the Appeals Chamber would, and the Prosecution is certainly not asking the Appeals Chamber to do so. I would then move on to the next ground of appeal, which is the unlawful confinement of civilians. Our response to this is very brief, and I think it's a point that we made earlier. Our position is not based on a standard of knowledge that Mr. Mucic ought to have known or is to be held against a standard of perfection, or anything like this. I said this, in our submissions, in relation to the appeal by Mr. Delic that our position is based on the finding that he had actual knowledge, and, therefore, the question of what the situation wouldn't be if he didn't have actual knowledge is not something that needs to be determined in this appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: May I just, before you proceed, say that if the transcript correctly records me, I had intended to say, "to make sure we take no notice of what was said in the judgement." I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: I have no further submissions, Your Honour, on those grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Morrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour, the point is, or one of the points is, that this ground of appeal, as far as the interviews are concerned, that we're dealing with a mixed question of fact and law. I've not gone into the facts. They're argued in the briefs. We don't, of course, because I didn't argue them, is simply because we've been enjoying not to argue the matters in the briefs, and I'm hopefully sticking reasonably loyally to that. Same for the question of whether or not the interpreter should have been called. We don't in any sense withdraw from that. But as far as it's a question of law, it can be a review on appeal, a de novo look at the law, to see whether or not the law which is being applied is the law which ought to be applied, and that is quintessentially a matter for an appellate tribunal. As far as the question of a voir dire is concerned, yes, you could have a voir dire that begs the question, with the greatest of respect: How valuable is a voir dire in a system where the finders of both fact of law are the same tribunal? You then impinge, I appreciate, on very delicate territory and very delicate ground, because everybody will draw a sudden breath and say, "Oh, are you possibly saying that professional judges can't distinguish between the two?" And no, one is not saying that at all. But what it's saying is that where those matters are to be tested, if it is possible, it is better that they are tested in front of two separate tribunals because they are separate issues which are being raised. One answer is this: that, to borrow from the French system of having a person equivalent to a juge d'instruction, and having a predetermination of matters on the voir dire, which never appeared before the Trial Chamber in any shape or form, if a determination is made to exclude evidence, you are then in the same position as a judge and jury trial, where matters on the voir dire are heard before the judge alone and the jury only get to find what is admissible. But because there is no system, or there hasn't been a practical system, it would not, of course, be right or proper, and I know this Court would not, in any sense, hold that against the defendant that he didn't, as it were, raise, or it wasn't raised on his behalf, that such a procedure should be followed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Morrison, my information is that it was raised at some stage during the trial -- whether it was in relation to this matter or not, I don't know -- that the existence of the procedure was certainly discussed during the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, it may be that a qualitative decision was made by then lead counsel. I can't go into his mind on that matter. I don't think there's anything else I wish to say, except my learned friend did say -- talked about the universal rights as far as -- or universal procedure. The most universal right is that of fairness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and at a very convenient time. We'll take the break now and resume at midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now to Mr. Delic's group of grounds. Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Karabdic is going to discuss all except Counts 46 and 47. I'll discuss those separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Karabdic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honour. In the proceedings before this Tribunal, it is a generally accepted principle that facts have to be established beyond any reasonable doubt. That is the standard applied here: beyond reasonable doubt. According to previous practice, facts are established beyond reasonable doubt when there is no doubt that can be based on reason. So it is allowed that some doubt may exist, but not a doubt that would be in accordance with the principle of intelligent reasoning and thought. In the Tadic judgement, in the first degree, it was said that if a consideration of the facts allows for two possibilities, then the possibility that is more favourable for the accused must always be adopted, and this is the principle that in continental law is called in dubio pro reo: in case of doubt, what is more favourable for the accused should be accepted. The task of the Defence is to show that the Prosecutor, in presenting their evidence, have not achieved this standard. In these appeal proceedings I will deal with the reasons in the judgement, in the first degree, that relates to the facts and I will show that the required standard of beyond reasonable doubt has not been achieved. I shall limit myself only to some facts from the judgement. I shall take some links from the chain of reasoning of the Trial Chamber in the proceedings in the first instance, and this will be enough to break the whole chain and to topple the whole construction of the reasoning in the first degree. As regards murder, Counts 1 to 4, I think that my client has been found guilty of participating in the murders of Scepo Gotovac and Zeljko Milosevic. Let me point out at once that no witness saw or testified to having seen those murders. There were no eyewitnesses to describe how those murders happened. The facts in the judgement are based on indicia, which in our opinion, have not been established beyond reasonable doubt, and taken together, they do not show that these murders have been proved according to that standard. As regards the murder of Scepo Gotovac in Counts 1 and 2, in this courtroom Esad Landzo, who at the trial proceedings admitted that he had murdered Scepo Gotovac, described how he had done it, with some other guards, and does not mention Hazim Delic in his confession. This confession before the Trial Chamber is the strongest possible evidence, and the Trial Chamber should have accepted it. In our opinion, the Trial Chamber was right in rejecting Landzo's testimony when he accused others, but these reasons do not apply when he himself made the confession and confessed to what he himself had done. This fact alone --

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to have to object at the moment. This is a misstatement of the evidence in the case and I'm going to want to voice my objection that that is a total misstatement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We are hearing Mr. Karabdic. It's a matter of argument. When you come to your appeal, if it's relevant, you may raise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This shows that as regards the participation of Hazim Delic in this murder, not only is there reasonable doubt, but we think that it has been shown that he was not there and that he did not commit this offence. The reasoning given by the Trial Chamber in its judgement as regards this murder, in our opinion, does not meet the requirement of beyond reasonable doubt. The Trial Chamber found, in paragraph 817 of the judgement, that Gotovac was first taken out and beaten in the afternoon, then returned to the hangar. After that, in paragraph 818, it states that several hours later, in the evening, he was again taken out of the hangar and then he was beaten by Delic and Landzo, so that two prisoners brought him into the hangar and that a badge had been stuck into his forehead and that he died a few hours later as a result. However, there is no proof, no evidence to prove beyond reasonable doubt that Delic was there at all when Gotovac was taken outside for the second time in the evening when he was beaten to death. In paragraph 814 of the judgement, it is stated that in support of the allegations made in these two counts of the indictment, the Prosecution called and examined 12 witnesses. Eight of those witnesses, Stefan Gligorevic, Witness N, Niko Djordjic, Witness B, Branko Sudar, Risto Vukalo, Rajko Draganic, and Witness R, all agreed in saying that Landzo then called out Gotovac's name and took him outside. It has no significance that Witness B thinks that Delic was near the door when Landzo called Gotovac. And when Draganic says that either Landzo or Delic may have participated in the fatal beating, Witnesses F and Dragan Kuljanin did not know who had called out Gotovac's name, while witness Branko Gotovac only supposed that it was Delic. Only witness Mirko Babic claimed that Delic had participated in the fatal beating, but the Trial Chamber did not give credence to that witness, even when he testified to his own injuries. And Articles 27, 28, and 29 of the indictment, paragraph 978 of the judgement, so that he could not be believed when he was talking about somebody else's injuries. Branko Gotovac and Sudar testified to having heard Landzo's voice outside the hangar. No one said that they heard Delic's voice outside the hangar. They all testified that this time Landzo, after the beating, brought Gotovac back to the hangar, except for witness Gligorevic, who did not know anything about it. I think that this shows sufficiently that the standard of beyond reasonable doubt has not been met and that, therefore, it is in the interests of justice that Delic should be acquitted of this crime. The second count of murder --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sorry. Before you proceed to the next one, you did say that Mr. Landzo had confessed to this crime and in the course of his confession he had not mentioned your client, Mr. Delic. Now, there is no reference to that in your submissions. Have you got a page reference to the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is -- yes, I can, Your Honour. Maybe not at this moment. Let me just have a look and I'll tell you. 15045 to 15046, 15047. So those three pages contain his statement that he killed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's the part that you rely upon?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Counts 3 and 4, he is accused of the death of Zeljko Milosevic, who died as a result of a beating. The Trial Chamber was convinced that the last beating caused the death of the victim, and this is stated in paragraph 833 of the judgement in the first instance. In paragraph 832, as regards all the events, the death of Zeljko and all the events leading to the death of Zeljko Milosevic, the Trial Chamber gave special credence to the testimony of Witness Novica Djordjic and Milenko Kuljanin.
