utterances.text: I believe it must have been taken into account in consideration with the Serbs, who were charged with more murders and more violations of cruel treatment and torture than Mr. Landzo was charged with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But who hadn't yet started their trials.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Had you finished? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, I've finished with that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: If you don't mind, I'll go to diminished --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, may we just take it one ground at a time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Staker.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: May it please the Chamber. The argument is being put that Mr. Landzo was a very low-level perpetrator. Now, as I understand the argument, it's not being put that it could be a ground of appeal, following a trial and conviction, that the perpetrator wasn't a sufficiently high-level perpetrator. We saw on the ELMO this document being put about the Tribunal being established to try only the most serious perpetrators, but I understand the argument is only being put on the basis of discrimination, that there's no argument being put that a ground of appeal would be that the perpetrator is not sufficiently serious.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. Staker.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: I thank my friend. If that's the case, though, it must be assumed that the Tribunal has the jurisdiction, and therefore the ability, to try perpetrators at all levels in the command, and I don't think there's ever been a suggestion that if there are sufficient reasons justifying it - and the discretion is one essentially within the Prosecutor to determine what indictments are presented for confirmation - that low-level perpetrators can [sic] be tried. And clearly it would be impossible for every alleged crime in the former Yugoslavia to be tried by this Tribunal, and that therefore there needs to be some selectivity and that prosecutions in this Tribunal will always be selective in some sense. There can be no objection to selectivity as such. The issue here is selectivity on an impermissible basis. Ms. Sinatra has put that Mr. Landzo was tried, while others who were identically situated were not tried. Now, as we have put in our response brief, and as has come out in argument just earlier, there can be no basis for the argument that Mr. Landzo was identically situated with those against whom the indictments were withdrawn, the simple reason being that he was at mid-trial, and it's a very different thing to withdraw an indictment when someone's already mid-trial to withdrawing an indictment against someone before trial has even commenced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Can you just help me, though, on one particular problem. Ms. Sinatra has gone beyond the 14 to which the Prosecutor has referred, and she says there were 16, and I assume that the other two were in custody but hadn't yet faced trial. It's anything but clear to me, at the moment, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: That is something that it might be possible to clarify after the next break. Certainly I don't think there's any suggestion that trials had commenced against any of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No. She has agreed with that. But she refers to the figure of 16. The previous Prosecutor talks about 14 and asserts that none of them had yet been arrested, which puts them on a completely different basis, I would have thought, with all due respect. But if there were two that were in custody who were also released with their -- the charges against him withdrawn, I think we should know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will attempt to clarify that, although I should specify that it would still be our submission that there's a difference between a person who's been arrested and whose trial has not yet commenced and a person who's at trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I understand that completely, but as I understand Ms. Sinatra's submissions, there is somebody, or at least two people, somewhere in between who were actually in custody but whose trial hadn't begun.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: I will endeavour to clarify that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I think, if I remember rightly, they were in custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I have to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Thank you. In any event, as we say, even if the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think the French translators are having trouble with you, probably with your speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: My sincerest apologies to the translators. I will endeavour to be slow. Even if the legal principles are as put by Ms. Sinatra, we submit that it's not the case that Mr. Landzo was identically situated to those against whom the indictment was withdrawn. But I would also like to address the question of the relevant legal principles. I come back to a point that I made earlier today. In the appeal brief that was filed on behalf of Mr. Landzo, reference is made to national law, and again it's a case where reference has been made to the national law of only a single jurisdiction. In this case it's that of the United States of America. As an aside, I would notice that it is the practice in this Tribunal, and the Prosecution's understanding, I believe, is that Rule 111 in fact requires, that copies of all authorities relied upon be filed with the appeal brief, and we note that that appeal brief filed on behalf of Mr. Landzo did in fact contain a copy of the Pinochet decision, but not of any of the United States authorities that were relied upon, and copies of these cases were subsequently provided in the book of authorities for the Prosecution's response brief. It's our submission that if the legal principles set out in those cases were taken as an adequate reflection or as an accurate reflection of the legal principles applying in this Tribunal -- and we don't concede that that's necessarily the case -- that they don't in fact support the argument being put here at all. I would refer to the case of United States versus Armstrong. That's referred to on page 15 of the Landzo appeal brief. And the case itself is reproduced, as I said, in the Prosecution's book of authorities. The relevant page is registry page number A2757, which sets out the principles. Briefly stated, it's said there that: "The Attorney General and the United States Attorneys, which means the Prosecutors in the United States system, "retain a broad discretion to enforce the Nation's criminal laws. As a result, the presumption of regularity supports their prosecutorial discretion [sic], and, in the absence of clear evidence to the contrary, courts presume that they have properly discharged their official duties." There then follows the statement which I think is the one relied upon by my colleagues for Mr. Landzo, which says that: "The decision whether to prosecute may not be based on an unjustifiable standard, such as race, religion, or arbitrary classification." The case then goes on to say that: "In order to dispel the presumption that a Prosecutor has not violated equal protection, a criminal defendant must present clear evidence to the contrary," and it adds that "The claimant must show [sic] that the federal prosecutorial policy had a discriminatory effect and that it was motivated by a discriminatory purpose." Then another case perhaps of relevance here as well is Oyler versus Boles, another case relied on in the appellant's brief, at page 13 of the brief. The relevant page is reproduced in the Prosecution book of authorities at registry page A5930 [sic]. And there it is said: "Moreover, the conscious exercise of some selectivity in enforcement is not in itself a federal constitutional violation." Even though the statistics in this case might imply 25 a policy of selective enforcement, it was not stated that the selection was deliberately based upon an unjustifiable standard such as race, religion, or arbitrary classification". Then in United States versus Parham -- this is not an United States Supreme Court decision, it's a Federal Circuit Court of Appeals reproduced at Registry page A2787 -- the Court of Appeal said that where a defendant cannot show anyone in a similar situation who was not prosecuted, he has not met the threshold point of showing that there's been selectivity in Prosecution. So if these principles are applied to the circumstances of this case, what's the result? As I've said, the position of Mr. Landzo was not identical to those against whom indictments were withdrawn, that whatever statistics might indicate, unless clear evidence is presented by Mr. Landzo that this was motivated by a discriminatory purpose, the standard set out in the United States cases is not met. Now apart from the argument based upon the withdrawal of the indictment against some accused, and as we say their position was not identical, the Landzo appeal brief contains a number of factual assertions. I refer to page 17 of that brief where it is said: "In order to give the appearance of even-handedness, the Prosecutor had to scour the countryside to find allegations of war crimes against those of all ethnic backgrounds." Now, if it's suggested that the Prosecution was scouring the countryside with a discriminatory purpose, I must say that it's something the Prosecution certainly has never conceded or admitted. The appellant pointed to no finding of the Trial Chamber to that effect, and I submit there's no basis for the making of that kind of accusation. I assume it's not an accusation made against the Prosecution on the basis of any evidence, but that this is merely an inference that's sought to be drawn from the withdrawal of certain prosecutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Surely, Mr. Staker, the proposition could only be made good if you looked at all the indictments that have been filed, because it's no part of the Prosecution's duties, unfortunately, to be able to arrest people. So the Prosecution has little to say in who comes to the Court to be tried. That depends upon who's picked up or who surrenders. So the issue would have to be determined in relation to the indictments that were filed. And there's no suggestion that there was such a scouring around of people against whom indictments could be filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Yes. And in any event, indictments themselves, the decision as to against whom indictments will be filed can be based on various perfectly legitimate considerations. Apart from the level in the hierarchy of the perpetrator or alleged perpetrator or indeed even the gravity of the crimes that were committed, it may include matters such as where the particular perpetrator fits in in relation to others who have been indicted. It may be that a low-level perpetrator provides the crime base for an allegation of superior responsibility against a higher-level perpetrator so that it would be necessary to bring evidence of the crimes committed by that person in order to establish the superior responsibility of another. The likelihood of an arrest being effected in the future may be a legitimate consideration in determining who will be indicted. And as I've said, these United States cases, though they support the proposition that a mere comparison of statistics is not sufficient to establish that there's a discriminatory purpose and that there has to be clear evidence of the actual motivation based on discrimination not a mere analysis of the relative numbers of those prosecuted. In fact, it would be our submission that what Ms. Sinatra really seems to suggest is that the Prosecution should be doing precisely what she says it can't, namely that where indictments are presented on the basis of what appear to be legitimate criteria but then there's an imbalance in the different numbers from different groups being indicted, that regardless of any merits, the Prosecution should then seek to find a few indictees to make up the balance to give an overall impression of even-handedness, and we would submit that that would be a greater injustice than what's being complained of here. Our submission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: With regard to this point, and perhaps you can answer this question, the fact that, as Ms. Sinatra mentioned, there are only three indicted Muslims, is it due to the fact that you only indicted three or only three were arrested?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: That's another matter, Your Honour, on which I would have to seek clarification. Perhaps I could answer that after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Unless there are further questions, I have no further submissions in relation to that ground of appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For my part, I have a question that I would like to put to the Prosecutor, but maybe that Ms. Sinatra could also listen to it and maybe try to answer it. What consequences do you draw from the fact that we find ourselves before an International Tribunal, the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia, which was created in the circumstances that we are all very well aware of, before a Tribunal who does not have exclusive jurisdiction on the different crimes that are of its jurisdiction, i.e., crimes against humanity, war crimes, genocide, among others, this Tribunal that doesn't have exclusive jurisdiction on the crimes committed, and it has a certain number of competencies described within its rationae temporis jurisdiction, crimes committed since 1991 and until the Security Council deems it's necessary to put an end to the Tribunal's function in terms of its rationae temporis jurisdiction. We don't have exclusive jurisdiction but we have primary jurisdiction; i.e., other Tribunals can been called upon to try the people who are prosecuted. Ms. Sinatra was comparing, when she was talking about selective prosecuting, what happens at the national level and what happens at the international level, which is not something that can be compared, in fact. I'm sorry to have to say that, but in these last two days I see many people trying to transpose what happens at a national level to what happens at the international level, and you do this very freely without taking the necessary precautionary measures. What happens internally has nothing to do with what happens internationally, even though a certain number of principles can apply at both levels. So the fact that some indictments have been dismissed as it has been explained to us, the fact that they have been withdrawn, so to speak, does not at all mean that these persons cannot be prosecuted anymore. These individuals can be prosecuted in other countries or, as the Prosecutor Arbour says, if is deemed necessary, the Prosecutor himself can prosecute them at a later stage according to the circumstances which prevail. So the principle of nondiscrimination which you have been mentioning does not apply in the same way. This is a power that was granted to the Prosecutor by the founding act of the Tribunal. The Prosecutor has jurisdiction to prosecute individuals of who it thinks that it is necessary that they be prosecuted in view of the evidence that it has in its hand, but that doesn't mean that the Prosecutor has to prosecute all the individuals who find themselves in the similar situation. That is the situation as it stands, and I would like both the Prosecutor's and the Defence's opinion on that fact. Now, trying to say things without taking the necessary precautionary measures when you speak about international law is something that might lead us to more confusion. Even though national jurisprudence and case law can be of use when you use it with all precautionary measures, but do not forget that you are in an international tribunal. This is what I wanted to say. Is there something that either of would you like to add? I'd be most interested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Staker?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Yes. In response to that question, I think it would be the Prosecution's position that that is certainly an additional consideration that applies in the case of this Tribunal that does not apply in the case of a national jurisdiction. I'm not sure that the Prosecution would want to push that argument to an extreme and say that no matter what, this could never be a consideration here, but I think certainly it's an additional factor. I think perhaps it's unnecessary to consider potential extreme cases in this instance, because, as I say, even if one applied the standards that have been applied in the national jurisdiction relied upon, this case simply doesn't fall within it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, if you wish to reply to Judge Bennouna and also to reply generally, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I will try to reply to both. Judge Bennouna, I believe you were talking about the primacy of the International Tribunal and also when we are trying to come up with standards of law to apply, since right now some of the issues we're dealing with, we're dealing with in a vacuum. We draw from all sources of legal answers that we can come up with, and if they happen to be a course of national law, we're here only to put these thoughts before the Tribunal. It's up to you to decide what standards, what laws you want to apply. There are no cases in international law that I can see dealing with selective prosecution, so we were left solely with national law to draw from. I don't know if that answered your question. I apologise for just citing United States law, but it was the one most available to me and the one I'm most familiar with when I'm in Texas or California, because I don't have access to the library here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but beyond that you have to look at what the Statute says and you have to look at all the articles, all the papers that have been written on the Tribunal and its jurisdiction. When we speak of primacy, when in fact the future International Criminal Court will have a concurrent jurisdiction and will not have a primary jurisdiction or prevailing jurisdiction, what we're looking at is what are the competencies of the Prosecutor basically. You can't have the Prosecutor being expected to draw indictments for all the people who would be susceptible to be brought before the Tribunal. He has to make a choice. This choice is made by taking into account a certain number of considerations which are those of the Prosecutor. But it is well understood that it doesn't mean that these individuals have been declared innocent by the Prosecutor by the simple fact that an indictment has not been brought against them. The individuals that are not prosecuted by the Prosecutor but who are presumed to have at least committed a certain number of serious offences can be prosecuted, as you well know, before any Tribunal in the world, and that is the principle of universal jurisdiction. That is the situation that we find ourselves in. So you should bear this this mind when you try to speak of selective prosecution, and which brings you to say that a person who has been tried and convicted should be released because the same standard that was applied to other people has not been applied to her. And you also refer to Article 21, an article that, let me remind you, deals with the way people should be tried, people who are accused individuals who are brought before us by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And it is my submission that although Mr. Staker argued that they were not in identical positions as Mr. Landzo, whose actual trial had commenced, I believe that the rule of law would embrace that trial. The trial process begins upon indictment, and if the trial process begins at indictment, then they were in the same shoes. And that's really all I have to add as far as -- well, also Mr. Landzo does agree with the Prosecution's position on US versus Parham, I believe you cited, which states the standard that we were looking for anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Ms. Sinatra, granting that they are in the same shoes, just to following your reasoning, don't you think there should also be an intention of discrimination, or would it be self-evident that if they're in the same shoes, discrimination is established?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe that there was any discrimination that had been established, but they were in the same shoes and they should have had equal treatment under Article 21. As far as what Judge Bennouna was just talking about, I believe he was talking about pre-indictment. I'm talking about post-indictment equality. And I'm not trying to limit the Prosecutor's right to indict whoever they have enough investigation against, but I'm talking about post-indictment treatment of the accused before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Let us -- there was also one of the reasons, I think, of the Prosecutor to, let's say, withdraw some indictments, was the economic factor which was said, but as far as having started the trial for half a year almost, don't you think the economic factor here is not equal? You are speaking of exactly equal conditions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I didn't know that we can equate economy in dollars or guilder to justice before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That is apparently what the Prosecutor had mentioned, that economically it would be better for the Tribunal to withdraw some indictments. But in that case, the trial was already -- economically speaking, it would not be on the same level if the policy was economic. I'm just commenting on the order or the statement of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: That's exactly what I meant. It's impermissible for the Prosecutor to maintain charges and convictions against one person who stands in the same shoes as others, and especially impermissible to do it for economic reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Does that conclude your submissions on your selective prosecution grounds?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, we've got three minutes, if you'd like to say something about diminished responsibility. I remind everybody that there is no late session today. We will not be sitting from 4.30 to 5.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, in that case, Your Honour, I would ask the Court's indulgence to allow me to begin the new issue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That seems fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'll adjourn and resume at 10 in the morning.
